stories.headline: NASDAQ 100 EDGES HIGHER ON NVIDIA STRENGTH WHILE S&P 500 SLIPS TO 7,324, EXTENDING FIVE-MONTH LOW
stories.body: The Nasdaq 100 rose 0.44% to 27,116 as Nvidia's post-earnings strength lifted mega-cap tech, but the S&P 500 fell 0.23% to 7,324, extending its slide from Tuesday's five-month-low close even after Nvidia's blowout Q3 print; the split shows one stock's beat wasn't enough to turn the broader tape.
stories.explain: The Nasdaq 100 is heavily weighted toward a handful of mega-cap technology names, so a single large beat from Nvidia can move the index's return meaningfully higher even while the broader, more sector-diverse S&P 500 stays negative. That divergence is a breadth signal: when an index's gain is concentrated in one or two names rather than broad-based buying, the rally sits on a narrower foundation that is more vulnerable to reversing once that one name's momentum fades.

stories.headline: WTI CRUDE TUMBLES 3.4% TO ~$82, GOLD SHEDS 1.6% AS GEOPOLITICAL RISK PREMIUM UNWINDS AND DOLLAR FIRMS
stories.body: WTI crude fell 3.36% to roughly $82 a barrel and gold dropped 1.56% to about $3,728 an ounce, as easing fears of a Strait of Hormuz disruption pulled the geopolitical risk premium out of oil while a firmer dollar (DXY +0.16%) weighed on gold.
stories.explain: Oil carries a 'risk premium' above the price implied by pure supply-and-demand fundamentals whenever a key chokepoint like the Strait of Hormuz faces disruption risk; when that risk recedes, traders unwind hedges and short the premium back out, producing an outsized one-day move with no change in actual barrels produced or consumed. Gold, priced in dollars, competes with Treasury yields for safe-haven capital, so a firmer DXY and a Fed still seen as more likely to hike than cut in December both raise the opportunity cost of holding a zero-yield asset.

stories.headline: DECEMBER HIKE ODDS HOLD NEAR 72-77% AS TRADERS AWAIT OCT. PCE NOV. 25, NOVEMBER JOBS DEC. 4
stories.body: Futures-implied odds of a quarter-point hike at the Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting held in the 72-77% range, little changed after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's recent public remarks, with the fed funds rate still at 3.75%-4.00% following October's 10-2 hold; the Oct. core PCE report on Nov. 25 and the November jobs report on Dec. 4 remain the key swing data before the decision.
stories.explain: Fed funds futures and swaps embed a probability-weighted average of possible outcomes, so when odds barely move after a Fed chair speaks publicly, the market judged the remarks as confirming rather than updating its existing view of the reaction function. With two inflation and labor-market releases landing in the eight days before the meeting, each will mechanically shift those implied odds by changing the probability-weighted path the futures curve prices in, which is why both dates sit atop trading desks' calendars right now.

stories.headline: ANTHROPIC SET TO BEGIN TRADING UNDER TICKER ANT ON NASDAQ THURSDAY, AFTER PRICING UP TO $1.4 TRILLION VALUATION
stories.body: Anthropic's IPO, priced at $70-$78 a share for a fully diluted valuation of up to roughly $1.4 trillion, is scheduled to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market Thursday, Nov. 19, under ticker ANT, with AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC separately committing $26 billion to a concurrent private placement.
stories.explain: A gap between pricing and the first trade is standard IPO mechanics — it gives underwriters time to allocate shares to institutional buyers before the stock opens to the public, which is also when real price discovery happens and the deal can trade meaningfully above or below its IPO price. The $26 billion in strategic private-placement demand from chipmakers and cloud providers is a direct read on AI capex conviction that investors will weigh against Nvidia's own guidance when ANT opens, since both are bets on the same underlying demand curve.

stories.headline: HUANG'S CONGRESSIONAL TESTIMONY DATE SLIPS FROM NOV. 18 TOWARD THANKSGIVING WEEK OR DEC. 1
stories.body: Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before House committees over his contacts with a Megaspeed executive flagged by U.S. intelligence, but the originally requested Nov. 18 closed-door briefing date has slipped, with House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast saying testimony will land before Thanksgiving (Nov. 26) and other reporting pointing instead to a Dec. 1 transcribed interview.
stories.explain: A voluntary closed-door briefing carries no subpoena deadline, so its date is a negotiation between committee staff and Huang's counsel rather than a fixed legal obligation, which is why the window has already moved from a specific day to a looser 'before Thanksgiving' commitment. For markets, the overhang persists either way: whenever the session happens, any disclosure about export-control or trade-secret risk lands on a stock still digesting a leadership transition, a blowout earnings print, and a compressing gross-margin guide, so the delay mainly extends the uncertainty rather than removing it.

watchlist: Oct. core PCE inflation data — Nov. 25, the last major print before the Fed's Dec. 8-9 meeting
November jobs report — Dec. 4, landing four days before the FOMC decision
Fed's Dec. 8-9 FOMC meeting — hike odds near 72-77% with the funds rate at 3.75%-4.00%
Anthropic's Nasdaq debut under ticker ANT — Thursday, Nov. 19, after pricing at $70-$78/share, up to $1.4 trillion valuation
Jensen Huang's House testimony — date now fluid, expected before Thanksgiving (Nov. 26) or as late as Dec. 1

deepDive.title: How a Geopolitical Risk Premium Gets Priced Into Oil — and Unwound in a Single Session
content: WTI crude fell 3.36% today to roughly $82 a barrel, a move too large to explain with any change in actual oil production or consumption over the past 24 hours. Nothing about global supply or demand shifted that fast. What moved was sentiment around the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint through which a large share of the world's seaborne oil passes, as fears of a disruption there eased. That gap between what fundamentals justify and what price actually does is the geopolitical risk premium — and today's drop is a clean example of it compressing in real time as traders repriced the odds of a worst-case supply shock.

The risk premium exists because oil markets price not just expected supply and demand but the probability-weighted cost of tail risk — a war, a blockade, a sanctions regime that could pull millions of barrels a day offline with little warning. Traders express that risk through futures curves and options skew: when fear rises, near-term futures and out-of-the-money calls (bets on a price spike) get bid up relative to what a pure supply-demand model would predict. When the fear recedes, as it did today with renewed talk of a deal easing Hormuz tensions, those same positions get unwound — sold back — and the premium evaporates just as quickly as it built, producing a sharp one-day move that has nothing to do with barrels actually extracted or burned.

What's easy to miss is how large and how fast these premiums can swing relative to the 'fundamental' price underneath them. After Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, oil roughly doubled within weeks on fear alone, then fell by half within months once the actual supply disruption proved smaller than feared. The September 2019 drone strikes on Saudi Arabia's Abqaiq facility knocked out about 5% of global supply overnight and sent Brent up nearly 15% in a single session — its largest one-day jump in decades — only to retrace most of that move within three weeks once Saudi output recovered faster than markets expected. In both cases, the premium moved before the barrels did, and unwound before the headlines faded.

That pattern matters for reading today's setup. A shrinking oil risk premium is disinflationary at the margin — lower energy costs feed directly into headline CPI and, with a lag, into the core PCE print due Nov. 25 that the Fed is watching closely ahead of its Dec. 8-9 meeting, where hike odds currently sit near 72-77%. It also helps explain why gold fell alongside oil rather than acting as a pure safe haven today: when geopolitical tail risk recedes and a hawkish Fed keeps real yields elevated, both assets lose part of their bid at the same time, for related but distinct reasons.
